items.title: Knowing the equations exactly doesn't let you predict the weather
items.claim: The atmosphere obeys Newton's laws, well-known fluid dynamics, well-known thermodynamics. Knowing all the equations doesn't let us predict beyond about 10 to 14 days. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.
items.prompt: How can determinism coexist with unpredictability?

options.text: In chaotic systems, infinitesimally different initial conditions diverge exponentially over time; predicting day 20 requires knowing today's conditions to a precision beyond physical measurement

items.reveal:
Edward Lorenz, simulating weather on a vacuum-tube computer in 1961, restarted a calculation from intermediate data printed to 3 decimal places. The internal precision was 6 places. The truncated and full simulations diverged completely within a simulated month.

He published the result in 1963 with a simplified 3-equation model showing strange attractor dynamics. His 1972 talk title — 'Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?' — gave us the butterfly effect.

The key insight: any uncertainty in initial conditions doubles every few days in the atmosphere. After 10 doublings — about 2 to 3 weeks — uncertainty in tiny details has grown to dominate the whole forecast.

Ensemble weather forecasting (running many simulations from slightly perturbed starts) addresses this by giving a probability distribution rather than a single prediction.
items.why: Determinism is conflated with predictability. Lorenz showed they are different: the equations may be exact and the system may still be unpredictable in practice, because small errors grow exponentially.

items.title: 45 degrees is only optimal for a projectile in a vacuum
items.claim: Every physics textbook says the maximum range for a projectile is at launch angle 45 degrees. True in vacuum. In real air, the optimum angle is significantly less — and for some launches it's barely above 30 degrees.
items.prompt: Why does air change the optimum?

options.text: It doesn't — 45 degrees is always optimal
Air resistance reduces both horizontal velocity and vertical velocity, but the loss to drag is greater on long airborne paths; lowering the angle reduces flight time and total drag exposure
Gravity is different at high angles

items.reveal:
Vacuum case: range = (v^2 / g) * sin(2 * theta). Maximised at theta = 45 degrees.

With linear drag (low-speed air): the optimum angle decreases with launch speed and drag coefficient. For a thrown baseball or shot put, optimum is ~42-43 degrees.

With quadratic drag (more realistic at high speed): for a golf ball, optimum is closer to 12-15 degrees (combined with backspin for lift). For an artillery shell, often 30-40 degrees due to high muzzle velocity and dense air.

Why: higher launch angles mean longer flight times, more time exposed to drag, more total energy lost. The trade-off between vertical reach and drag loss shifts the optimum downward.

For a long-jumper, who launches around 7-10 m/s, the optimum angle calculated from biomechanics is ~22 degrees, not 45 — because the long-jumper cannot achieve high vertical velocity from horizontal sprint and because air resistance is minor. Body-mechanics constraints matter more than the equation.

The 45° result is a useful first approximation but should not be taken as universal. Most real-world projectile design uses computational fluid dynamics rather than analytical formulas.
items.why: Textbook results assume ideal conditions. In real applications (golf, baseball, artillery, athletics), the answer is shifted — often substantially — by drag and biomechanical constraints. 'Theoretically 45°' is correct for nothing on Earth.

items.title: A thrown ball at 10 m/s reaches the same height regardless of angle
items.claim: Throw a ball straight up at 10 m/s: it reaches 5.1 metres. Throw it at 45 degrees with horizontal speed component 7.07 m/s and vertical 7.07 m/s: the vertical component alone determines max height (2.55 m). The horizontal speed is irrelevant to height.
items.prompt: Why doesn't horizontal velocity affect maximum height?

options.text: Horizontal and vertical motions are INDEPENDENT (Galileo's insight). Gravity only acts vertically; horizontal velocity remains constant (in vacuum) and contributes nothing to vertical position. Maximum height depends only on initial vertical velocity component
Horizontal motion adds to height through Pythagoras

items.reveal:
Galileo's insight (~1604): motion can be decomposed into independent perpendicular components. Vertical motion under gravity proceeds the same way regardless of horizontal motion.

For a projectile launched at speed v at angle theta above horizontal:
- Horizontal velocity: v * cos(theta), constant in vacuum.
- Vertical velocity: v * sin(theta) initially, decreasing under gravity.
- Max height: h = (v * sin(theta))^2 / (2g). Independent of horizontal component.
- Range (in vacuum): R = v^2 * sin(2 * theta) / g.
- Time aloft: t = 2 * v * sin(theta) / g.

Dropping a bullet and firing it horizontally simultaneously: they hit the ground at the same time (assuming flat ground, no air resistance). The horizontal motion of the fired bullet doesn't change its vertical fall. This was first demonstrated experimentally by Galileo's student Vincenzo Viviani.

Mythbusters tested this with .45 caliber bullets (S07E11): bullet dropped vs bullet fired horizontally landed almost simultaneously (with millisecond-scale differences from air, recoil, ground curvature).

Applications:
- Artillery: vertical and horizontal trajectories computed separately, then composed.
- Skydiving: horizontal travel during fall depends on jump speed; vertical fall time depends only on altitude.
- Sports: free throws, basketball shots, soccer kicks — coaches train the vertical component for height and arc, horizontal for distance.

With air resistance, the decomposition is not exact — drag depends on total velocity, mixing the components. But the vacuum result is the framework.
items.why: Motion in two directions seems like it should interact. Galileo's discovery that perpendicular motions are independent is one of the deepest simplifications in physics — and the reason projectile problems are solvable at all.
